nameStory: This snail earned its 'giant' title honestly - it's one of the largest land snails in the world, growing to impressive sizes that dwarf our native New England snails. The 'African' part tells us where it originally comes from, though like many invasive species, it has spread far beyond its homeland in East Africa.
description: The African Giant Snail is a massive land snail that's dramatically larger than any native New England species. These invasive mollusks have large, conical shells that can grow quite substantial, making them unmistakable when encountered. They're voracious eaters that consume plants rapidly and are considered serious agricultural pests wherever they establish. In New England, they're extremely rare due to our climate, but any sighting should be reported immediately as they're federally prohibited.

idTips.label: Shell Size
idTips.description: Enormously larger than any native snail - the shell feels substantial and heavy in your hand, with a dramatic conical shape that towers over typical garden snails

idTips.label: Shell Pattern
idTips.description: Shell shows distinctive brown and cream banding or mottling, often with a glossy appearance when the snail is healthy and active

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: The soft body is typically grayish or brownish, feeling smooth and very muscular to the touch - much more substantial than our small native snails

idTips.label: Feeding Signs
idTips.description: Leaves large, distinctive feeding holes in plants with smooth, rasped edges from their powerful feeding apparatus

idTips.label: Slime Trail
idTips.description: Creates thick, wide slime trails that feel notably more substantial and sticky than the delicate trails left by native snails

habitat: In New England, these snails cannot survive our winters outdoors and would only be found in heated greenhouses, indoor plant collections, or as escaped pets during warm weather. They prefer mild, humid conditions and would gravitate toward areas with abundant vegetation and shelter from temperature extremes.

seasonality.spring: Any outdoor sightings would likely occur in late spring when temperatures warm up, possibly near greenhouses or in areas where they might have been accidentally introduced with imported plants.
seasonality.summer: Most active period if present, when they would be feeding voraciously on garden plants and leaving obvious damage and slime trails.
seasonality.fall: Activity would decrease as temperatures drop, and they would seek shelter in warm, protected areas like greenhouses or heated buildings.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters outdoors - any winter sightings would be in heated indoor environments like greenhouses or homes.

funFact: These snails are so destructive that they're banned at the federal level in the United States - possession can result in serious legal consequences, and agricultural inspectors take sightings very seriously as potential ecological disasters.
confusionNotes: Nothing in New England even comes close to this snail's massive size - if you find a snail that seems impossibly large compared to our native species, you've likely found something that shouldn't be here. Remember: when in doubt, don't touch, and report it to authorities immediately.
contextualKnowledge: This species is federally prohibited in the United States, meaning it's illegal to possess, sell, or transport them. They're considered one of the world's most destructive invasive species and can carry parasites that affect human health. Any sighting should be reported to state agricultural authorities.
compareHints: Since there are no other giant African snails established in New England, compare this to our largest native species like the white-lipped snail - the African Giant Snail will be dramatically larger, often several times the size. The size difference alone is so striking that confusion with native species is unlikely once you see one.
